newsitem.title: UK: Hospital slip-ups make falling ill risky business.
newsitem.headline: Hospital slip-ups make falling ill risky business.

text.p: Going to hospital can be a risky business, according to a new study which shows that mistakes by hospital staff are much more common than previously thought.
Researchers in the United States spent nine months closely monitoring three surgical units in a large teaching hospital and spotted errors in the care of more than 45 percent of patients.
At least four out of the 1,047 patients in the study died because of hospital mistakes and in 17.7 percent of the cases, patients suffered serious effects such as temporary disability.
The specially-trained team joined the teaching rounds in the hospital, followed the junior doctors' rounds and monitored nurses' shift changes and other meetings where patients' care was discussed.
Writing in the Lancet medical journal, Professor Lori Andrews of the Chicago-Kent College of Law, said most of the errors happened during the daily care of patients rather than in surgery.

Nearly 38 percent of mistakes were down to one individual, 15.6 percent were due to faulty interaction between staff and 9.8 percent were caused by administrative botches, such as failing to provide necessary equipment or enough staff.
Most patients who fell victim to such mistakes had to spend longer in hospital and so their medical costs were increased.
The longer a patient was in hospital, the more likely they were to fall victim to an error.
"The likelihood of experiencing an adverse event increased about six percent for each day of hospital stay," said Andrews.
Surprisingly, said Andrews, despite the portrayal of patients in the United States as over-litigious, only a tiny proportion of the victims in the study, 1.2 percent, made compensation claims.
Four years after the study of the 13 patients who made claims, three had received compensation, eight claims had been dropped and two were still pending.

The study showed a much higher rate of hospital errors than any previous investigation has done. This was largely because data in other studies usually came from hospital records which often failed to mention errors in treatment.
